 Incumbent Mayor Ken Welch (right) and political veteran Charlie Crist are running for the St. Pete mayoral post. (FILE IMAGES) 
 Crist, Welch vie to lead St. Petersburg into the future
 BY 
 Rod Gipson
 Pinellas County 
 UPDATED 11:24 AM ET Nov. 03, 2026 
 PUBLISHED 8:57 AM ET Oct. 28, 2026 
 PUBLISHED 8:57 AM EDT Oct. 28, 2026 
 SHARE 
 ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — As Election Day arrives, both incumbent Mayor Ken Welch and political veteran Charlie Crist continue to maintain that their campaign is best suited to run the city.
 Some polls suggest Crist, the state’s former governor, attorney general, state senator and congressman, has an edge heading into Nov. 3.
 Elections in Tampa Bay: Here's what you need to know 
 Meanwhile, both have laid out their vision for the future of St. Pete.
 Issues include fortifying the city against future storms, affordable housing, economic opportunities and the ongoing questions of redeveloping the Gas Plant District once the Rays complete a move to Tampa.
 Welch, mayor since 2022, has been pushing for a plan that could cost roughly $275 million. The project has been in the works for years in different forms.
 The 2024 storms, Helene and Milton, also remain big topics. There is a referendum on the St. Pete ballot that, if approved, would create an additional property tax to support $600 million in bonds to address stormwater projects and would speed up the timeline.
 “You cannot just wish this away,” Welch, 62, said during a recent Spectrum News debate of a push to strengthen the city to storms. “You can’t just kick the can down the road. The next storm that comes, we will have the same problems if we don’t make the investment.
 “We are doing everything we can through our water rates and stormwater rates, which we don’t want to raise even higher.”
 There also have been issues within the administration.
 From the dual hurricane’s aftermath to a failed Rays stadium deal in St. Pete, the administration has faced criticism. Welch has responded that it was his leadership that brokered a deal to get Tropicana Field refurbished in time for the 2026 season and now has been featured on a national World Series stage.
 Crist, 70, meanwhile, has faced his own criticism for party switching and being accused of being a political opportunist.
 Crist has said that the City of St. Petersburg’s spending is out of control and that he could have done a better job keeping the Rays on the Pinellas side of the Bay area.
 “The last thing I want to do is burden you with a bond that has more debt on the City of St. Petersburg than we have right now,” Crist said. “We need to live within our means. I think a lot of these issues should have been addressed earlier.”
 The property tax issue, Amendment 3, also has been a talking point.
 St. Pete says it is estimated to lose $33 million in property tax revenue starting in 2028 if it passes, and $54 million the following year.
 Both agree it would be bad for the city. Crist said he wants to cut property taxes by $15 million, but Welch disagrees with Crist’s plan.
 “The truth is, all of our property taxes do not pay for police and fire by themselves,” Welch said. “So you are going to have to cut other things or cut police and fire, as he did when he was governor.”
 Crist said: “Amendment 3, if it were to pass, it would be like a sledgehammer to cities, to counties all over the state of Florida. And I’m for property tax reduction, but not to the degree that this one would hammer all of us with.”
